html:
The Battle of Ipsus was fought in 301 BCE near the town of Ipsus in Phrygia, in the west of today's Turkey. A coalition of the former generals of Alexander the Great beat and killed Antigonus the One-Eyed, the strongest of them.

After Alexander died, his generals fought over his empire in the Wars of the Diadochi. Antigonus, who ruled most of Asia Minor and Syria, and his son Demetrius wanted to reunite it under themselves. Cassander of Macedon, Lysimachus of Thrace and Seleucus of Babylon joined forces to stop them. Seleucus brought about 400 war elephants, which he had been given by Chandragupta Maurya. Demetrius broke the cavalry in front of him and chased it too far. Seleucus then moved his elephants across to block his return. Antigonus, left without cavalry, was surrounded and killed, aged about 81.

Ipsus ended the last real attempt to hold Alexander's empire together. The winners divided the lands of Antigonus. Out of the division came the lasting kingdoms of the Hellenistic age: the Seleucid Empire in Asia, Ptolemaic Egypt, and Macedon.
